source_review.notes: Checked all eight references for identity, edition or revision, and cited scope. Fowler's Continuous Delivery definition supports deployability on demand and the distinction that continuous deployment automatically puts qualifying changes into production; his 2024 Continuous Integration revision supports the preceding integration practice. Humble and Farley supports deployment-pipeline, build-once, environment, migration, and release-mechanism foundations. Google SRE Release Engineering supports exact build identity, policy gates, push-on-green versus selected releases, automation, and risk-matched rollout; the SRE Workbook Canarying Releases chapter supports bounded comparative rollout and cautious causal interpretation. Verified Accelerate and Continuous Delivery bibliographic metadata, current Continuous Delivery Foundation glossary identity, and NIST SP 800-218 Version 1.1 release and provenance scope. Current sources checked 2026-09-06.

evidence: Defined artifact and time domains, deployment contexts, identity, evidence, policy, recoverability, deployment policy, deployment and release predicates, and bound authorization tuple before use.
Checked conjunction, function domains and codomain, membership, non-implication, tuple notation, equality language, and every GitHub math delimiter.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Readiness is explicitly time- and context-dependent rather than a permanent property of an artifact.

evidence: Executed delivery-deployment-state-model under CPython 3.14.4 and matched seven exact output lines with empty stderr and exit status zero.
Checked two of three candidates satisfy evidence, policy, and recoverability, so delivery_ready contains r17 and r19 and continuous_deployment_count is 2.
Checked r18 has failed evidence and therefore failed_candidate_deployed is false.
Checked deployed code true versus feature enabled false produces feature_release_equals_deployment false, and rollback operation deploy produces the stated equality true.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Counts and Boolean states are illustrative and do not measure a delivery organization.

evidence: Expanded readiness as the conjunction of immutable identity, valid evidence, policy satisfaction, and recoverability and checked any false term makes the predicate false.
Checked deployment policy maps artifact, time, and context to deploy, hold, or deny and requires readiness for every deploy result.
Checked deployment does not imply feature release by construction and that release may occur through activation without new code deployment.
Checked changing any authorization tuple field changes the bound subject and requires re-evaluation.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The predicates organize decisions; they do not claim a decision procedure can prove universal production correctness.

evidence: Reviewed continuous integration, delivery, deployment, release, staging, release candidates, release trains, business cadence, emergency paths, and automatic safety holds.
Reviewed exact artifacts, mutable tags, rebuilds, configuration, multi-service manifests, evidence expiry, vulnerability changes, target drift, waivers, stale approvals, and concurrent controllers.
Reviewed feature flags, disabled and enabled paths, flag-service failure, cleanup, external APIs, expand-and-contract data migration, irreversible side effects, rollback and roll forward.

Reviewed canary attribution, low traffic, delayed failure, missing telemetry, incident state, error budgets, offline clients, mobile distribution, safety-critical systems, partial rollout, duplicate requests, and break-glass response.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: The chapter explicitly permits manual authority where judgment is real while treating deterministic manual mechanics as delivery debt.

evidence: Traced every readiness and deployment decision to immutable source, artifact, configuration, environment, evidence, policy, time, approval, and recovery identities.
Checked a manual release decision in continuous delivery never substitutes for missing technical evidence.
Checked continuous deployment automatically acts only on qualifying ready subjects and enters explicit hold states during unsafe context.
Checked deployment and user-facing release remain separate transitions with independent observation and recovery.
Checked normal, emergency, rollback, and roll-forward operations use the same rehearsed controlled mechanism.
invariant_checking.notes: Deployment frequency is never treated as sufficient evidence of continuous-delivery capability.

evidence: Reviewed the capability implication and confirmed trustworthy continuous deployment requires continuous-delivery readiness while continuous delivery permits policy hold.
Reviewed subject binding and confirmed changed artifact bytes, configuration, environment, policy, or decision time invalidates prior authorization as applicable.
Reviewed the flag-disabled deployment counterexample and converse activation case, establishing deployment-release non-equivalence.
Reviewed readiness non-monotonicity under expiry, vulnerability disclosure, drift, incidents, and policy change.
proof_review.notes: Arguments establish relationships among defined states and do not claim operational implementations are formally verified.

evidence: Audited uses of continuous, ready, safe, successful, verified, exact, every, automatic, deploy, release, rollback, guarantee, and proof.
Confirmed formal predicate results, foundational source definitions, current guidance, professional policy, hypothetical cases, and local executable evidence are distinguished.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Canary observation is explicitly bounded evidence and a stop decision is not presented as causal proof.

evidence: Executed the sole practical snippet under CPython 3.14.4 with declared exact stdout, empty stderr, and exit status zero.

Confirmed readiness filters failed evidence, manual delivery approval is independently represented, automatic deployment selects both ready candidates, feature release differs from code deployment, and rollback uses the deployment mechanism.
Confirmed all monthly, quarterly, canary, mutable-tag, feature-flag, migration, dependency, emergency, mobile, and metric cases are hypothetical teaching situations.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No real artifact, pipeline, deployment controller, feature service, database migration, production canary, user release, rollback, or delivery organization was exercised or measured.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed the full distinction from integration through sustained deployability and automatic production policy, with explicit delivery units, readiness, evidence versus authorization, automated mechanisms, deployment versus release, progressive exposure, manual and automatic policy, environment limits, observation, and pipeline testing.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed failures involving stabilization phases, manual deterministic work, monthly and train batching, mutable tags, post-approval rebuilds, broad release manifests, stale evidence, hidden waivers, database and API incompatibility, flag debt, canary attribution, unsafe rollback, emergency bypass, telemetry loss, controller retries, active incidents, offline clients, and frequency gaming. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified undergraduate progression from precise continuous-practice vocabulary through four predicates and four bounded arguments, one executable seven-outcome state model, eight trade-off pairs, eighteen misconceptions, ten distinct worked situations, and five exercises progressing from distinctions through readiness evaluation, diagnosis, policy comparison, and offline-device transfer.

limitations: Internal authoring, source, mathematical, executable-model, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed. Foundational books and articles, current guidance, a deterministic state model, and hypothetical cases do not establish that any real product is continuously deliverable, safe to deploy automatically, recoverable, correctly authorized, sufficiently observable, compatible across versions, or valuable to users.
